2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The polarity finding in ANSD has to be read through the time course of the two generators that can appear on a click ABR.

The cochlear microphonic is an AC outer hair cell receptor potential. It is stimulus-following and polarity sensitive, so condensation and rarefaction invert, and it is pre-neural and stimulus locked. With a brief click that contribution is essentially confined to the very early cochlear window, roughly the first ~≤1 ms post onset, and then it decays with the stimulus. A true neural ABR I-V is essentially polarity insensitive; in normal hearing after that early microphonic artefact window the condensation and rarefaction averages are superimposable and the reproducible I-III-V complex dominates.

In ANSD outer hair cell transduction is essentially intact so OAEs and a CM are preserved, whereas phase-locked neural synchrony from the inner hair cell ribbon synapse onward is lost or grossly desynchronised. The functional picture is therefore an absent/non-reproducible polarity insensitive I-III-V at high intensity with preserved OAEs/CM, often with at best an isolated/variable Wave I and absent/grossly abnormal III-V.

On separate polarity averages what can remain recordable is the preserved polarity-sensitive receptor activity. That activity can only be mirrored while it is physiologically present. With a brief click the CM is essentially confined to the very early cochlear window, ~0-≤1 ms post onset, and then decays with the stimulus. PRIVATE REFLECTION: The pathophysiology is settled: ANSD = preserved cochlear outer hair cell transduction → preserved OAEs, cochlear microphonic/summating potential, with loss/gross desynchronisation of phase-locked neural synchrony distal to the inner hair cell ribbon synapse → absent/non-reproducible/grossly abnormal polarity-insensitive I-III-V ABR at high intensities, often at best an isolated/variable Wave I, absent/malformed III-V, with preserved OAEs/CM. Options A and B are agreed non-specific: peaks 1+3 present/V absent and simple prolongation of peaks 1/3 latency at 95 dBnHL are not defining.

The remaining dispute is the operational vs physiological description of the polarity test.

CM is an AC outer hair cell receptor potential: stimulus-following, polarity sensitive, inverts condensation↔rarefaction, pre-neural and stimulus-locked. With a click it is essentially confined to the early cochlear window ~0-≤1 ms post onset and then decays. A true neural ABR I-V is essentially polarity insensitive; in normals the small polarity-sensitive CM contribution is limited to ≤1 ms, after ~1 ms condensation and rarefaction averages are superimposable and polarity invariant. Alternating polarity averaging cancels CM and leaves neural ABR in normals.

In ANSD the reproducible polarity-insensitive brainstem generator is absent/desynchronised. Alternating polarity averaging therefore cancels CM and leaves essentially no response. What can remain on separate polarity averages is the preserved polarity-sensitive receptor activity. That activity can only produce an inversion/mirror while it is physiologically present.

D camp, now numerical majority in round 3, Colleagues 1,10,11,12,13,14,16,17,18,19,2,20,21,3,4,5,6,7,8,9:
* Mirror image is limited to the CM time course, i.e. brief early ≤1 ms stimulus-locked window. Beyond ~1 ms there is no reproducible polarity-invariant neural waveform; waves III-V are absent/non-replicable and trace is essentially flat/non-reproducible/noise.
* A sustained mirror >1 ms would require a sustained polarity-sensitive generator lasting several milliseconds, which the brief stimulus-locked CM does not do.
* The “prolonged >1 ms mirror” phrasing is operational shorthand for failure of the normal post-~1 ms polarity convergence when neural ABR is absent, not evidence the CM itself persists for several ms.

C camp, Colleagues 11,12,15,8 in earlier rounds and residual operational teaching:
* With neural component lost the recording stays dominated by polarity-following receptor activity and condensation remains essentially mirror image of rarefaction well beyond ~1 ms, i.e. prolonged phase reversal >~1 ms for whole trace.
* This is taught as classic electrophysiologic marker of loss of neural synchrony.

Unresolved wording tension: textbook “prolonged mirror >1 ms” is operationally intended as failure of post-~1 ms polarity convergence; physiologically the polarity-sensitive signal being mirrored is the brief CM limited to ≤1 ms. Most colleagues now favour the physiologically literal description D, i.e. short early ≤1 ms mirror image with loss of later reproducible polarity-invariant waves III-V, with preserved OAEs/CM. The strictly correct functional statement “absent/non-reproducible neural ABR with preserved OAEs/CM” is not perfectly captured by any A-D, hence residual appeal of E, but of the morphologic options D best matches known CM time course.

I previously leaned to C based on conventional teaching; repeated physiological clarification about CM time course has shifted my weight toward D, while retaining note of the operational C shorthand. Current best answer among options is D, with caveat that E is the ideal functional description.

Functionally that is an absent/non-reproducible polarity-insensitive I-III-V at high intensities with preserved OAEs/CM, often at best an isolated/variable Wave I.

Where the polarity test matters is which generator is actually being mirrored. The cochlear microphonic is an AC outer hair cell receptor potential. It is stimulus-following and polarity sensitive so condensation ↔ rarefaction invert, it is pre-neural and stimulus locked, and with a click it is essentially the duration of the stimulus itself, i.e. confined to the very early cochlear window ~0-≤1 ms post onset and then it decays. A true neural ABR I-V is essentially polarity insensitive. In normal hearing the small polarity-sensitive CM contribution is cancelled on alternating-polarity averaging and from ~1 ms onward condensation and rarefaction averages are superimposable and dominated by reproducible Waves I-V.

In ANSD the reproducible polarity-insensitive brainstem generator is absent/desynchronised. Alternating polarity averaging therefore cancels the CM and leaves essentially nothing. What can remain on separate polarity averages is the preserved polarity-sensitive receptor activity. That activity can only produce an inverted/mirror relationship while it is physiologically present. So on separate condensation vs rarefaction averages you see a mirror image only for the duration of the CM itself, the brief early ≤1 ms stimulus-locked window. Beyond ~1 ms there is no reproducible polarity-invariant neural waveform to sustain a brainstem response; Waves III-V are absent/non-replicable and the record is essentially flat/non-reproducible noise rather than a sustained coherent inverted waveform.

A sustained mirror image >1 ms for the whole recording window would require a sustained polarity-sensitive generator lasting several milliseconds out to the latency range of III-V. The CM is not sustained in that way; it follows fine structure and decays within the first millisecond. The clinical teaching of a “prolonged” mirror or loss of normal post-~1 ms polarity convergence is an operational shorthand for the fact that the neural ABR that would normally rescue polarity invariance after ~1 ms is missing. It is a description of the failure of convergence, not evidence that the microphonic itself persists as a coherent polarity-following source for several ms.

That is why the morphologically faithful polarity correlate is an early, brief ≤1 ms condensation-rarefaction inversion due to CM contamination with loss of later reproducible polarity-invariant Waves III-V at 95 dBnHL despite preserved OAEs/CM. A and B are not the specific ANSD polarity signature. The functionally ideal statement remains absent/non-reproducible neural ABR with preserved OAEs/CM, but of the morphologic descriptions offered the CM-window limited early mirror with loss of later neural waves is D.

I am settling on D as the best morphologic description among the options given, with the caveat that the truly principled functional statement is E.

The physiology is a cochlear-to-neural dissociation. Outer hair cell transduction is essentially intact so OAEs and a cochlear microphonic / summating potential are preserved, whereas the reproducible polarity-insensitive neural generator for a normal I-III-V is absent / grossly desynchronised. Functionally that is an absent / non-reproducible / grossly abnormal polarity-insensitive ABR at high intensity, often with at best an isolated / variable Wave I and absent / malformed III-V, with preserved OAEs/CM.

The polarity test separates pre-neural from neural contributions.

* The cochlear microphonic is an AC outer hair cell receptor potential. It is stimulus-following and polarity sensitive so condensation ↔ rarefaction invert. It is pre-neural and stimulus-locked and with a click it is essentially confined to the very early cochlear window ~0-≤1 ms post onset and then decays.
* A true neural ABR I-V is essentially polarity insensitive. In a normal ear the small polarity-sensitive CM contribution is cancelled on alternating polarity averaging and from ~1 ms onward condensation and rarefaction averages are superimposable and polarity invariant.

In ANSD the reproducible polarity-insensitive brainstem generator is lost / desynchronised. Alternating polarity averaging therefore cancels the CM and leaves essentially no response. What can remain on separate polarity averages is the preserved polarity-sensitive receptor activity.

That activity can only produce an inverted / mirror relationship while it is physiologically present. On separate condensation vs rarefaction averages you therefore see a mirror image only for the duration of the CM itself, i.e. the brief early ≤1 ms stimulus-locked cochlear window. Beyond ~1 ms there is no reproducible polarity-invariant neural waveform to sustain Waves III-V; the record is essentially flat / non-replicable noise.

A sustained mirror image >1 ms would require a sustained polarity-sensitive generator lasting several milliseconds out to the latency range of III-V. The CM is stimulus-locked and decays within the first millisecond. The “prolonged mirror >1 ms” phrasing is an operational bedside shorthand for failure of the normal post-~1 ms polarity convergence when the neural ABR is absent, not evidence that the CM itself persists for several ms.

Options A and B are not the specific ANSD polarity signature. The morphologically accurate polarity correlate of preserved cochlea with loss of neural synchrony is the short early ≤1 ms condensation-rarefaction inversion due to preserved CM with loss of later reproducible polarity-invariant waves III-V at 95 dBnHL despite preserved OAEs/CM. That is D.

Strictly functionally the ideal statement remains absent/non-reproducible neural ABR with preserved OAEs/CM, which is not perfectly captured by A-D, i.e. E, but of the morphologic options given D best matches the known ≤1 ms CM time course.

PRIVATE REFLECTION: The deliberation remains anchored on ABR polarity physiology in auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder. Stable consensus across rounds:

* Outer hair cell transduction / OAEs / cochlear microphonic / summating potential typically preserved.
* Neural synchrony / phase-locking of auditory nerve-brainstem is lost or grossly desynchronised.
* Cochlear microphonic is an AC receptor potential, stimulus-following and polarity sensitive, inverts condensation ↔ rarefaction; true neural ABR I-V is polarity insensitive after the early cochlear window.
* Normal ear: small polarity-sensitive CM contribution in ~0-≤1 ms, then condensation and rarefaction averages are superimposable / polarity invariant. Alternating polarity averaging cancels CM and leaves neural ABR.

Options A and B are rejected by the group: ANSD is not characterised by selective preservation of peaks 1 and 3 with peak 5 absent up to 95 dBnHL, nor by simple prolongation of peaks 1 and 3 latency at 95 dBnHL.

Round 4 public responses converge on D as the physiologically accurate morphologic description, with explicit caveat about E as the ideal functional statement.

Core reasoning repeatedly restated:
* With loss of reproducible polarity-insensitive neural generator, alternating polarity averaging cancels CM and leaves essentially no response.
* What remains on separate polarity averages is preserved polarity-sensitive receptor activity.
* That activity can only produce an inverted/mirror relationship while physiologically present. CM with a click is stimulus-locked and essentially confined to ~0-≤1 ms post onset and then decays.
* On separate condensation vs rarefaction averages the traces are mirror images only for the duration of the CM itself, i.e. brief early ≤1 ms stimulus-locked window. Beyond ~1 ms there is no reproducible polarity-invariant neural waveform to sustain Waves III-V; record is flat/non-replicable at 95 dBnHL despite preserved OAEs/CM.
* A sustained mirror image >1 ms would require a sustained polarity-sensitive generator lasting several ms out to III-V latencies, which the CM does not do.

The “prolonged >1 ms mirror” wording is now consistently framed as operational bedside shorthand for failure of normal post-~1 ms polarity convergence when the neural ABR is absent, not evidence of a physically prolonged CM. Operationally you read loss of convergence and essentially absent/non-reproducible ABR after the early window. Physiologically the mirroring is limited to ≤1 ms CM time course with loss of later reproducible polarity-invariant waves III-V.

C camp minority position is retained in memory: operational teaching describes persistent polarity-sensitive waveform well beyond normal ~1 ms CM window, i.e. prolonged phase reversal >~1 ms for whole recording window with absent/non-reproducible I-III-V despite preserved OAEs/CM, and ≤1 ms mirror image is normal CM alone.

E as principled fallback is repeatedly noted: the ideal functional statement is absent/non-reproducible neural ABR with preserved OAEs/CM, which is not perfectly captured morphologically by any A-D.

Current weighting: overwhelming round 4 majority D holds for physiologic accuracy of the polarity test – early brief ≤1 ms condensation-rarefaction inversion due to preserved CM with loss of later reproducible polarity-invariant waves III-V. C is retained as operational shorthand for loss of post-~1 ms polarity convergence. E remains the strictly correct functional description. I continue to track both interpretations and keep E in mind as the ideal statement.

The pathophysiology remains stable and is now unanimous in the group: ANSD / auditory dyssynchrony = preserved cochlear outer hair cell transduction → preserved OAEs and a preserved cochlear microphonic / summating potential, with loss / gross desynchronisation of phase-locked neural generation distal to the inner hair cell ribbon synapse → absent / non-reproducible / grossly abnormal polarity-insensitive I-III-V ABR at high intensity, typically at best an isolated / variable Wave I with absent / malformed III-V, despite preserved OAEs/CM.

A = Peaks I and III present, V absent and B = prolonged latencies of peaks I and III at 95 dBnHL are rejected as specific ANSD signatures. No one supports them in round 4.

Polarity separation is the operant test:
* Cochlear microphonic = AC outer hair cell receptor potential, stimulus-following, polarity-sensitive, inverts condensation ↔ rarefaction, pre-neural and stimulus-locked. With a click it is essentially confined to the very early cochlear window ~0-≤1 ms post onset and then decays.
* True neural ABR I-V is essentially polarity-insensitive. In normal hearing the small polarity-sensitive CM contribution is cancelled on alternating polarity averaging and from ~1 ms onward condensation and rarefaction averages are superimposable and polarity invariant.

In ANSD the reproducible polarity-insensitive brainstem generator is absent / desynchronised. Alternating polarity averaging therefore cancels the CM and leaves essentially no response. What can remain on separate polarity averages is the preserved polarity-sensitive receptor activity.

That activity can only produce an inverted / mirror relationship while it is physiologically present. On separate condensation vs rarefaction averages the traces are mirror images only for the duration of the CM itself, i.e. the brief early ≤1 ms stimulus-locked window. Beyond ~1 ms there is no reproducible polarity-invariant neural waveform to sustain Waves III-V; the record is essentially flat / non-replicable noise.

A sustained mirror image >1 ms would require a sustained polarity-sensitive generator lasting several ms out to the latency range of III-V. The CM is stimulus-locked and decays within the first millisecond. The “prolonged >1 ms mirror” wording is now widely acknowledged in the group as operational bedside shorthand for failure of the normal post-~1 ms polarity convergence when the neural ABR is absent, not evidence that the microphonic physically persists for several ms.
